analysis.one_liner: Makes court sanctions for frivolous filings mandatory and requires violators to pay the other side's legal fees.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 228-195 on November 14, 2013, but it died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal Rule 11, the rule against frivolous court filings, so that judges would have to punish any lawyer or party who files a frivolous claim or defense. Sanctions would have to compensate the injured party, including attorneys' fees, and the bill would remove the 21-day window that currently lets a lawyer fix or withdraw a bad filing to escape punishment. It passed the House but never received a vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: If it became law, the main beneficiaries would be civil defendants — typically businesses, insurers, and institutions — who could recover attorneys' fees and costs whenever a court finds a plaintiff's or lawyer's filing violates Rule 11. Lawyers and law firms that file sanctioned papers would pay out of pocket, with mandatory rather than discretionary penalties. Individuals who sue large companies, and the plaintiff lawyers who represent them, would gain only where filings were genuinely frivolous, but would face a higher risk of paying the other side's fees if a judge disagrees with a claim's legal basis.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Corporate and insurance defendants in lawsuits

how_it_helps.text: Makes sanctions mandatory rather than discretionary whenever a court finds a party or attorney violated Rule 11's ban on frivolous filings.
Requires that any sanction compensate the injured party, including reasonable attorneys' fees and costs, and allows extra penalties such as striking pleadings or dismissing the suit.
Eliminates the 21-day safe harbor, so a sanction motion can be filed even if the challenged filing is promptly withdrawn or corrected.

analysis.who_pays: Lawyers and their clients whose filings are judged frivolous would pay the other side's fees and possibly penalties. Because sanctioned filings carry personal financial risk, plaintiffs' lawyers would become more cautious, which means people with strong but hard-to-win claims — in employment, civil rights, and consumer cases — would find it harder to get representation.

drawbacks.text: Removing the 21-day safe harbor means a lawyer can be sanctioned even after promptly withdrawing or correcting a flawed filing, punishing honest mistakes instead of only bad-faith claims.

Making sanctions mandatory, including paying the other side's attorneys' fees, will make lawyers more reluctant to take on contested cases; that burden falls hardest on people suing large companies who can outspend them in fee fights.
The bill applies across the board, so the same mandatory sanctions and fee awards can be used against plaintiffs in civil rights, employment, and consumer cases, not only against frivolous suits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's goal — fewer frivolous filings and making rule-breakers pay — is legitimate, and the burden falls on lawyers, not the public directly. But the design is blunt: removing the 21-day safe harbor punishes lawyers for correcting mistakes, and making sanctions automatic plus fee-shifting will scare lawyers away from taking hard cases, including the ones ordinary people bring. In practice the benefit flows to big defendants and the cost is weaker access to court. The House passed it on a near-straight party-line vote and the Senate never acted on it, so it never became law.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it along near-straight party lines, but the Senate Judiciary Committee never took it up, so it expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: On November 14, 2013, a Democratic motion to recommit — which would have exempted civil rights and constitutional cases from the bill — failed 197-225, with only one Republican voting for it.
The House then passed the bill 228-195, with 225 of 230 Republicans voting yes and only 3 of 200 Democrats voting yes.
The bill was received in the Senate on November 18, 2013, read twice, and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where no further action was taken before the 113th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary litigants and their lawyers are better off that the bill died, since mandatory sanctions and fee awards would have raised the risk of suing a well-funded opponent. Businesses and insurers avoid nothing but also lose nothing, since current Rule 11 already allows sanctions.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ordinary litigants; the bill never became law

for.name: Rep. Lamar Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through the House Judiciary Committee to passage.

for.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and business tort-reform groups
for.what_they_did: Long advocated mandatory Rule 11 sanctions as part of tort reform.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill after House passage and never took it up, letting it die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Rep. John Lewis
against.what_they_did: Offered a motion to recommit that would have exempted civil rights and constitutional cases from the bill; it failed 197-225.

against.name: Trial lawyers' bar and civil justice consumer groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill, arguing it would chill legitimate lawsuits.

sides.party_line_note: The vote split almost perfectly by party: 225 of 230 Republicans voted yes and only 3 of 200 Democrats did; the Democratic motion to recommit got just one Republican vote.

industries.industry: Large corporations and insurers as civil defendants
industries.note: As the most frequent targets of lawsuits, they gain a tool to recover legal fees from anyone who sues them and loses a Rule 11 argument, and the chilling effect on plaintiffs' filings reduces their litigation exposure.
The mandatory sanction and fee provisions and the loss of the safe harbor expose them personally to paying opponents' fees, which discourages taking on risky cases against well-funded defendants.
They gain a fee-shifting weapon when their clients win sanctions motions, but face the same mandatory sanctions when their own filings are found frivolous.
